chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam or someone else, from Sayf ibn Ameyra, from a man, from Jabir, from Musafir, from Bishr ibn Ghalib al-Asady, from al-Husayn ibn Ali (peace be upon him) who said:

Whoever recites a verse from the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic, during his salat while standing, one hundred good deeds are written for him for every letter. When he recites it outside of salat, God writes ten good deeds for him for every letter. If he listens to the Quran, God writes one good deed for him for every letter. If he completes the Quran at night, the angels pray over him until morning. If he completes it during the day, the guardian angels pray over him until evening, and he has an answered supplication, and it is better for him than all that is between the sky and the earth.

I said, 'This is for the one who recites the Quran. What about the one who does not recite?' He said: 'O brother of the clan of Asad! God is Generous, Glorious, and Benevolent. When he reads whatever he has (of the Quran), God gives him that (reward).'

key_terms.الحفظة: The guardian/recording angels (hafaza), who record human deeds
key_terms.حسنة: Good deed, merit; a unit of divine reward (hasana) recorded by the angels
key_terms.دعوة مجابة: An answered supplication; one whose prayer will be accepted by God
key_terms.كتاب الله عز وجل: The Book of God, Mighty and Majestic — a standard epithet for the Quran

ai.seo_question: What are the rewards for reciting the Quran during prayer according to Imam al-Husayn?
ai.summary: Imam al-Husayn ibn Ali (AS) enumerates a hierarchy of spiritual rewards for engaging with the Quran: recitation during prayer (100 good deeds per letter), recitation outside prayer (10 per letter), listening (1 per letter), and completing the Quran at night or day (angelic prayers). Crucially, when asked about those who cannot recite, the Imam emphasizes God's generosity — even a person who recites whatever portion of the Quran they know receives the same divine reward. This teaching reflects the Shia emphasis on accessibility of divine grace and the meritorious nature of all sincere engagement with the Quran, no matter how limited.
